fixes.explanation: Yes, it's false, baker. The verse says, “Genuine righteousness leads to life, but the pursuit of evil brings death.” Genuine righteousness leads to life. The pursuit of evil brings death, so it doesn't lead to life.

Wandering is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't say it. Solomon says, “Be assured that the wicked will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will escape.” The two halves sit side by side: the wicked will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will escape.
Ruling is a big promise, and the verse doesn't make it. Solomon says, “…but the offspring of the righteous will escape.” He sets that against the wicked, who will not go unpunished.

That's what the verse says, baker. “One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor.” Two people are set side by side. The one who gives freely gains even more, and the one who withholds what is right becomes poor.
It's actually true, baker. Solomon says, “He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like foliage.” The man trusting in riches falls, and the righteous thrive like foliage.

That's it, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), writes, “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD…” Shaving a few crumbs off every sale might feel tiny, but the verse doesn't treat it that way. He's serious about honest dealing.
I bet pride expects applause, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “When pride comes, disgrace follows…” Disgrace is what follows, not praise.

Strength is a sensible guess, but it isn't what this verse names. Verse 7 says the hope of the wicked man's strength vanishes. Solomon says in verse 4, “…but righteousness brings deliverance from death.”
Not quite, friend. The verse says, “…but the wicked fall by their own wickedness.” It names their own wickedness as what they fall by. It doesn't mention anyone tripping them.
Right, it's false, baker. The verse says, “…but the wicked fall by their own wickedness.” It names their own wickedness, and it says nothing about someone else tripping them.

That's the word. The verse says, “The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the faithless are trapped by their own desires.” The upright are delivered by their righteousness. The faithless are trapped by their own desires.

A record sounds close, but it isn't the word. The verse says, “…but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.” A confidence is something someone trusted them with. Keeping it is what sets the trustworthy person apart from the gossip.

That's right. The verse says, “He who puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer, but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” One will surely suffer. The one who hates indebtedness is secure.
Solomon never calls that person lonely. He says, “…but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” He sets that against “He who puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer…”

Watchful sounds sensible, but it isn't the word. Solomon says, “…but the one who hates indebtedness is secure.” He puts that against the one who puts up security for a stranger, who will surely suffer.

Power isn't what Solomon names here. He says, “A gracious woman attains honor, but ruthless men gain only wealth.” The two are set side by side. She attains honor, and the ruthless men gain only wealth.
Yes, the twist! The verse says, “A kind man benefits himself, but a cruel man brings trouble on himself.” The kind man is the one who benefits. The cruel man brings trouble on himself.
Thank isn't the word. The verse says, “The people will curse the hoarder of grain, but blessing will crown the one who sells it.” Blessing crowns the one who sells it, and the hoarder gets cursed.

I wish that worked, but the verse says the opposite. Solomon says, “He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like foliage.” The man who trusts in his riches falls, while the righteous thrive.
Ruling over his own house isn't what the verse says about the fool. Solomon says, “…and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.” Servant to the wise of heart is where the verse puts him.

Rich is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't say it. Solomon says, “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise.” It calls the one who wins souls wise, and wealth isn't mentioned.
